claims.text: Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 initially exists as a high-temperature single-phase BCC alloy.
The phases appearing during cooling and thermal exposure are driven by ordering-induced, diffusion-mediated decomposition of the BCC phase.
Atomic-size mismatch, notably that associated with Al, produces local lattice distortions.
Differential elemental diffusivities combine with lattice distortions to promote chemical ordering and elemental partitioning.
During slow cooling or moderate annealing, chemical fluctuations overcome an interfacial-energy barrier and nucleate secondary ordered phases.
Ordered B2 or FCC phases can emerge from the original BCC matrix.
Annealing in the range 600–800 degrees Celsius should provide sufficient opportunity for diffusion and ordering.
The mechanism operates when cooling is sufficiently slow for diffusion and local chemical ordering to develop.
Extreme quenching suppresses the proposed diffusion-mediated ordering and decomposition.
Temperatures too low for appreciable atomic mobility suppress the proposed mechanism.
Local chemical order and size-mismatch lattice distortions drive elemental partitioning.
Local strain and chemical inhomogeneity produce differential diffusion that allows selected elements to segregate.
Elemental segregation promotes short-range ordering and lowers free energy through secondary-phase nucleation.
The interplay between elastic strain energy and diffusion gradually transforms metastable BCC material into a multiphase microstructure.
A rapidly quenched Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 baseline remains homogeneous BCC without detectable local ordering or precipitation.
Slowly cooled or annealed samples will contain secondary phases detectable by diffraction or microscopy relative to the quenched baseline.
Secondary-phase features will correlate spatially with local compositional fluctuations.
Reducing the alloy's atomic-size mismatch would significantly reduce the ordering driving force and limit applicability of the mechanism.
The identity and fraction of secondary phases may depend on composition and cooling or annealing schedules.
Failure to detect either secondary phases or local ordering in treated samples relative to the quenched control would falsify the hypothesis.
